title: Turtle Bell Push

image.credit: Cleveland Museum of Art, The India Early Minshall Collection (1966.473)
image.license: Public domain. Released under the Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access program

altText: A small decorative object in the form of a turtle, made from agate, gold, silver, diamonds and rubies.

source.verifiedBy: Cleveland Museum of Art open-access API record (title, creator, date, medium, culture, credit line, description, did_you_know, CC0 status, image URL)

context: A decorative bell push in the form of a turtle, made in St. Petersburg, Russia, by the House of Fabergé around 1895-1915 and now in the Cleveland Museum of Art. The museum lists agate, gold, silver, diamonds and rubies, and says a push on the turtle's head would ring a bell to summon the butler.

descriptions.k: This is a tiny turtle that is also a bell button. It is made from shiny stones and metals. A push on its head rang a bell. Where is the turtle's head? Where would you push?
descriptions.g12: This turtle is a bell push. A person pressed its head, and a bell rang downstairs to call the butler. It was made in Russia from stones and metals. Look closely at the turtle. Which parts look carved, and which parts look shiny?
descriptions.g35: This turtle was made in St. Petersburg, Russia, by the House of Fabergé around 1895 to 1915. The museum says a quick push on its head rang a bell downstairs to call the butler. It is made of agate, gold, silver, diamonds and rubies. Why make an ordinary button look like a turtle?
descriptions.g68: The House of Fabergé made this bell push, a useful object shaped like a turtle, in St. Petersburg around 1895 to 1915. The museum says Fabergé often used native hardstones for luxurious desk accessories, and that pushing the turtle's head rang a bell to summon the butler. How does this object combine function and decoration?
descriptions.g910: This turtle bell push by the House of Fabergé uses agate, gold, silver, diamonds and rubies. The museum says Fabergé craftsmen used the colors and textures of stones from the Ural Mountains, and that native materials appealed to the tsar and his family. How does this object blend craft, luxury and everyday use?
descriptions.g1112: The Turtle Bell Push turns a servant-summoning device into a luxury object of agate, gold, silver, diamonds and rubies. The museum notes Fabergé's use of native hardstones from the Ural Mountains and the appeal of such materials to the tsar and his family. What does the contrast between a humble function and precious materials suggest about the culture that valued it?

teacherNote.context: A bell push in the form of a turtle, made in St. Petersburg, Russia, by the House of Fabergé around 1895-1915 and now in the Cleveland Museum of Art. The museum lists agate, gold, silver, diamonds and rubies, and says a push on the turtle's head would ring a bell downstairs to summon the butler.
directions: Have students sketch an everyday button or switch redesigned as an animal, and explain how it would still work.
Ask older students to discuss how an object can be both useful and decorative, using this bell push as evidence.
Discuss why the museum's list of materials matters and what questions it leaves open, such as which part is made of which material.
